subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 52-year-old woman presents for a routine health examination. She has soft, painless, yellowish plaques on both upper eyelids that have slowly enlarged over several years. The remainder of the skin and eye examination is unremarkable, and she has no tendon nodules.
question: Which of the following best describes the composition of these lesions?

options.text: Lipid deposit within the Achilles tendon
Plaques composed of lipid-laden histiocytes in the skin
Proliferation of smooth muscle cells in dermal arterioles
Fibrinoid necrosis of the periorbital vessels

explanation_correct: Xanthomas are plaques or nodules composed of lipid-laden histiocytes in the skin. When they occur on the eyelids they are called xanthelasma, which is exactly this patient's presentation. They are a recognized sign of hyperlipidemia, although isolated xanthelasma can also occur in normolipidemic individuals.

explanation_incorrect.A: A lipid deposit in the cornea describes corneal arcus, a grayish ring around the corneal periphery, not yellow eyelid plaques.
explanation_incorrect.B: A lipid deposit within the tendon, especially the Achilles tendon and finger extensors, describes tendinous xanthoma, which presents as firm tendon nodules rather than soft eyelid plaques.
explanation_incorrect.D: Smooth muscle cell proliferation in small vessels describes hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis of severe hypertension, a vascular lesion, not a cutaneous plaque.
explanation_incorrect.E: Fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles is seen in hypertensive emergency, not in eyelid xanthelasma.

educationalObjective: Recognize xanthelasma as xanthomas of the eyelids composed of lipid-laden histiocytes in the skin.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 38-year-old man presents after twisting his ankle playing basketball. On examination, both Achilles tendons are firm and nodular, and similar nodules are palpable over the extensor tendons of his fingers. His father died of a myocardial infarction at age 44. His total cholesterol is 340 mg/dL and his LDL cholesterol is 275 mg/dL.
question: The nodules found on this patient's tendons are most strongly associated with which of the following?

options.text: Cholesterol embolization from an aortic plaque

explanation_correct: Tendinous xanthoma is a lipid deposit in tendon, especially the Achilles tendon and finger extensor tendons, and is classically associated with familial hypercholesterolemia. The markedly elevated LDL and the father's death from myocardial infarction at age 44 fit the autosomal dominant familial hypercholesterolemia phenotype, which carries a high risk of premature coronary artery disease.

explanation_incorrect.B: Diabetic microangiopathy produces hyaline arteriolosclerosis and retinopathy/nephropathy, not lipid deposits within large tendons.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hypothyroidism can cause secondary dyslipidemia, but the classic association of tendinous xanthoma is with familial hypercholesterolemia, and hypothyroidism is not suggested by this vignette.
explanation_incorrect.D: Firm nodular thickening of the Achilles and finger extensor tendons is not a normal age-related change; it reflects lipid deposition within tendon.
explanation_incorrect.E: Cholesterol embolization from aortic plaques causes livedo reticularis, blue toes, and organ ischemia after vascular procedures — not discrete tendon nodules.

educationalObjective: Associate tendinous xanthoma (Achilles and finger extensor tendons) with familial hypercholesterolemia.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 28-year-old man is noted during an eye examination to have a grayish ring around the periphery of each cornea. He also has nodular thickening of his Achilles tendons and an LDL cholesterol of 290 mg/dL. His 32-year-old brother has similar corneal findings.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's corneal finding?

options.text: Calcium deposition in the superficial cornea
Cholesterol embolization to corneal vessels from an aortic plaque
Lipid deposit in the cornea, common in older adults but appearing earlier in life with hypercholesterolemia
Corneal scarring from recurrent herpes simplex keratitis

explanation_correct: Corneal arcus is a lipid deposit in the cornea. It is common in older adults (arcus senilis), but when it appears earlier in life it signals hypercholesterolemia. This young man's arcus, together with tendinous xanthomas, marked LDL elevation, and an affected sibling, indicates a hypercholesterolemic state rather than benign age-related arcus.

explanation_incorrect.A: Copper deposition in Descemet membrane produces a Kayser-Fleischer ring seen in Wilson disease, not the lipid ring of corneal arcus.
explanation_incorrect.B: Calcium deposition in the superficial cornea causes band keratopathy, typically associated with hypercalcemia or chronic ocular disease, not hyperlipidemia.
explanation_incorrect.C: Cholesterol emboli from aortic atherosclerosis cause retinal and digital ischemia (eg, blue toes), not a peripheral corneal ring; the cornea is avascular in its central stroma.
explanation_incorrect.E: Herpetic keratitis causes corneal scarring with reduced sensation and visual deficit, not a symmetric peripheral gray ring associated with lipid abnormalities.

educationalObjective: Recall that corneal arcus is a lipid deposit common in older adults but appears earlier in life with hypercholesterolemia.
